planets.name: HD 189733 b
planets.hook: A blue planet with a very different atmosphere
planets.intro: HD 189733 b is blue in reflected visible light. It circles its star in just over two days, surrounded by a hot atmosphere where telescopes have detected water vapour, carbon monoxide and hydrogen sulfide.
planets.question: How did we find out that it is blue?
planets.answer: Hubble measured how much visible light disappeared when the planet passed behind its star. More of the missing light was blue than red. This gives us a colour without a resolved photograph of the globe.
planets.interior: Atmosphere → increasingly dense hydrogen–helium envelope → deep compressed fluid → possible heavy-element-rich centre. Use blended boundaries through the envelope.
planets.evidence: Visible-light secondary eclipses constrain reflected colour. JWST transmission spectra identify molecular absorption as starlight passes through the atmosphere.
planets.limits: A blue colour is supported. Exact clouds, their geography and glass rain are not directly measured. Keep the famous sideways-glass-rain story out of the main copy.

planets.name: HD 209458 b
planets.hook: An atmosphere revealed by a trace of sodium
planets.intro: HD 209458 b is a hot gas giant with sodium in its atmosphere. The sodium absorbs a small part of the starlight passing through the gas. This was the first exoplanet whose atmosphere was detected and chemically identified.
planets.question: How can a trace of sodium reveal a whole atmosphere?
planets.answer: Atoms absorb particular colours of light. When the planet crossed its star, the dip in brightness was slightly deeper at sodium’s wavelengths. Comparing neighbouring wavelengths isolated the extra absorption.
planets.interior: Hydrogen–helium atmosphere and deep fluid envelope, with a schematic heavy-element interior. Avoid an abrupt gas-to-solid boundary.
planets.evidence: The original Hubble transit measurement compared the sodium band with adjacent bands. Later spectroscopy probes water and atmospheric motion.
planets.limits: Use the sodium observation as the historical hook. Detailed colours and cloud structure are an illustration. Do not reproduce an unverified visible comet tail.

planets.name: WASP-39 b
planets.hook: A giant with the mass of Saturn
planets.intro: WASP-39 b has roughly the mass of Saturn, spread across a globe larger than Jupiter. Its hot, hydrogen-rich atmosphere contains water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Beneath the clouds, the gas grows denser with depth, with no solid ground to stand on.
planets.question: What does the carbon dioxide do?
planets.answer: Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light, so it changes how heat moves through the atmosphere and escapes to space. Water vapour and other gases do this too. The amount of carbon dioxide matters, but it cannot tell us the whole climate on its own. This planet has a deep hydrogen-rich envelope.
planets.interior: Extended atmosphere → hydrogen–helium envelope growing denser with depth → modelled heavy-element interior. Do not translate atmospheric metallicity into a measured core radius.
planets.evidence: JWST transmission spectra show a carbon-dioxide band and sulfur-dioxide absorption. Photochemical calculations explain how the sulfur dioxide can form.
planets.limits: Photochemistry is supported by spectra and modelling. The visible cloud colour is not a measured portrait.

planets.name: WASP-107 b
planets.hook: Clouds made from rock minerals
planets.intro: WASP-107 b has an enormous atmosphere for its modest mass. Almost as wide as Jupiter, it has only about a tenth of Jupiter’s mass. Its clouds contain tiny silicate particles, made from the same family of minerals that forms much of Earth’s rock. Here, that material hangs high in a hot atmosphere.
planets.question: What keeps the cloud material aloft?
planets.answer: Atmospheric mixing can carry vapour and tiny particles upward. Cloud models reproduce the silicate feature when that mixing is included. The same atmosphere contains much less methane than simple equilibrium chemistry predicts.
planets.interior: Cloudy atmosphere → extended hydrogen–helium envelope → hotter compressed fluid → substantial modelled core. Show that an apparently fluffy planet can contain a dense interior.
planets.evidence: MIRI probes the silicate absorption feature. Near-infrared spectra constrain gases, and coupled models connect their abundances to mixing and internal heat.
planets.limits: Different models infer different mixing strengths and abundances. Do not combine their numbers into one exact interior. “No methane” applies to an earlier dataset, not the later NIRSpec detection.

planets.name: WASP-43 b
planets.hook: Clouds on the night side
planets.intro: WASP-43 b completes an orbit in about 20 hours and is expected to keep the same side facing its star. Its day-side atmosphere reaches roughly 1,250 °C, while even the night side is around 590 °C. Thick clouds probably cover the darker hemisphere, hiding the hotter gas below.
planets.question: How do we study the night side?
planets.answer: As the planet travels around its star, different parts of its globe face us. Following the changing infrared brightness lets astronomers compare the day and night hemispheres.
planets.interior: Atmosphere → dense gas and fluid hydrogen–helium → uncertain central heavy-element region. Keep the thermal pattern in the atmosphere, not as a split core.
planets.evidence: JWST followed the planet through a full orbit. Its infrared brightness corresponds to about 1,250 °C on the day side and 590 °C on the night side in the measured wavelength range. Models with thick night-side clouds fit the faint night-time emission. The clouds block light from deeper, hotter layers. They can also trap heat, so faint emission does not mean the clouds cool the whole atmosphere. The climate models assume synchronous rotation.
planets.limits: Brightness temperatures describe the emitting atmosphere in a wavelength band. They are not ground temperatures. Exact cloud shapes are not mapped.

planets.name: WASP-121 b
planets.hook: Rock ingredients in gas form
planets.intro: The day side of WASP-121 b is so hot that some ingredients of rock remain in gas form. Its atmosphere contains silicon monoxide, a gas made of silicon and oxygen. The cooler night side contains methane, giving this giant different mixtures of gases on opposite sides.
planets.question: Can an atmosphere stretch around an orbit?
planets.answer: Helium observations detect absorption over a large fraction of the orbit. They support an extended outflow from the planet, far beyond the part of the atmosphere seen during an ordinary transit.
planets.interior: Very hot atmosphere → extended hydrogen–helium envelope → dense deep fluid → unresolved central composition. Add an upper-atmosphere escape illustration only in the evidence panel.
planets.evidence: Day- and night-side spectra identify gases. A separate full-orbit helium observation probes escaping material.
planets.limits: The helium signal is not a visible-light trail. Do not promise measured rain made of gemstones. Retain distinctions between lower-atmosphere chemistry and the escaping upper gas.

planets.name: WASP-17 b
planets.hook: Tiny quartz particles above a giant planet
planets.intro: WASP-17 b is nearly twice as wide as Jupiter, with less than half its mass. Tiny quartz particles form clouds high in its atmosphere. These crystals are far smaller than grains of sand, suspended above a vast envelope of hot gas.
planets.question: Quartz clouds?
planets.answer: Quartz has a characteristic infrared absorption feature. JWST measured extra absorption near 8.6 micrometres, and models containing very small quartz particles fit that feature better than the tested alternatives.
planets.interior: Thin high cloud layer → hydrogen–helium envelope → deep dense fluid → modelled heavy-element interior. Quartz stays in the cloud layer.
planets.evidence: JWST measured an infrared feature near 8.6 micrometres. Models with tiny quartz particles reproduce its shape. Grant et al. adopt a radius of 1.932 Jupiter radii and a mass of 0.477 Jupiter masses, the consistent pair used for the introduction. The archive table below preserves its separately sourced values.
planets.limits: The quartz identification comes from cloud models fitted to the spectrum. Particle size depends on the model. The introduction uses the mass and radius adopted together in Grant et al. (2023), rather than combining them with the different archive mass. Resolve the catalogue parameter choice before publication.

planets.name: GJ 1214 b
planets.hook: A world hidden by aerosols
planets.intro: GJ 1214 b is wrapped in thick clouds and haze that reflect much of its star’s light. They conceal a deep atmosphere and whatever lies beneath it. A water-rich interior is one possibility, with water buried under pressures far beyond those in Earth’s oceans.
planets.question: Why can a spectrum look almost flat?
planets.answer: High clouds and haze can block our view of deeper gas. They reduce the differences between wavelengths, leaving a much flatter transmission spectrum.
planets.interior: Aerosol-rich atmosphere → dense volatile envelope → possible water-rich deep region → rock and iron interior. Present this as a family of structures, not one measured ocean.
planets.evidence: Transmission data show muted features. Thermal phase-curve observations constrain reflection and heat transport. Later analyses adjust the inferred albedo and possible molecular signatures.
planets.limits: The 2024 carbon-dioxide and methane features need confirmation. A later ground-based non-detection does not by itself refute those weaker space-based features.

planets.name: LHS 3844 b
planets.hook: A dark rocky surface
planets.intro: A year on LHS 3844 b lasts about 11 hours. This small rocky world appears to have little atmosphere, leaving its surface exposed to its nearby star. Dark rock such as basalt could cover the ground, either in solid slabs or broken down into weathered dust.
planets.question: Can a telescope tell one rock from another?
planets.answer: Different minerals emit infrared light differently. Comparing the measured spectrum with laboratory rock spectra lets astronomers test possible surface materials. Several dark, low-silica materials fit this planet.
planets.interior: Rocky surface → silicate mantle → iron-rich core. Use the new mass constraint to discuss possible core fractions without claiming a unique structure.
planets.evidence: JWST emission spectroscopy is compared with laboratory mineral spectra. Independent radial-velocity studies now constrain the planet’s mass.
planets.limits: The spectrum does not uniquely choose basalt or establish that all of the surface is old. Fresh slabs and weathered powder can both fit. No accumulated volcanic gases were detected.

planets.name: TOI-561 b
planets.hook: A small hot planet that may have kept its atmosphere
planets.intro: TOI-561 b circles its star in less than 11 hours. A thick atmosphere may surround this intensely heated rocky world, above an ocean of molten rock. Gases dissolved in the molten interior could be released into the air, helping replenish what escapes to space.
planets.question: How could an atmosphere survive here?
planets.answer: Molten rock can store gases and exchange them with the atmosphere. Evolution models find some routes that preserve a thick atmosphere, although many starting conditions leave the planet bare.
planets.interior: Thick volatile atmosphere → magma ocean → deeper mantle → comparatively small core in some models. Avoid fixed pressure and exact core dimensions in the first illustration.
planets.evidence: JWST measured a dayside emission spectrum cooler than the tested bare-rock scenarios. Coupled interior–atmosphere models explore how such an envelope might survive.
planets.limits: CO2-rich and SO2-rich atmospheres are modelling possibilities, not two measured compositions. The 2026 survival paper is a recent preprint.

planets.name: Kepler-16 b
planets.hook: Two stars in the sky
planets.intro: Kepler-16 b travels around two stars in a 229-day year. The planet is similar to Saturn in mass and size. Its two suns move around each other while the planet follows a much wider path.
planets.question: Would the two suns always set together?
planets.answer: Their positions change as they orbit one another. From the planet, the two stars would move relative to each other in the sky. A specific sunset sequence also depends on the planet’s rotation and the observer’s location.
planets.interior: Cloudy atmosphere → hydrogen–helium envelope → deep compressed fluid → substantial heavy-element interior allowed by its density.
planets.evidence: Kepler recorded the planet crossing both stars as well as eclipses between the stars. These events constrain the masses and orbits.
planets.limits: Do not assign a known day length or sunset duration. The discovery constrains a gas giant, so a Tatooine-like desert is the wrong setting.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 b
planets.hook: The hot inner world of a compact family
planets.intro: TRAPPIST-1 b is the innermost of seven known planets around a tiny, cool star. Its hot day side and much colder night side suggest exposed rock with little atmosphere to carry heat between them.
planets.question: Why compare it with its neighbours?
planets.answer: The planets formed around the same star but receive different amounts of light. Comparing them helps test how small rocky worlds lose or retain their atmospheres.
planets.interior: Rock surface → mantle → possible iron-bearing core. Use mass and radius constraints shared with the system study.
planets.evidence: Transit timing constrains mass and radius. Thermal phase curves measure the difference between day and night emission.
planets.limits: No substantial atmosphere is favoured, but the illustration must not imply a measured crater map. The daytime temperature is a band brightness temperature.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 c
planets.hook: A rocky neighbour with a different heat signal
planets.intro: TRAPPIST-1 c is almost Earth-sized, with a year lasting just 2.4 days. Strong starlight heats this rocky world. Its surface may be bare, or covered by a thin atmosphere, with brighter rock reflecting more light than on its inner neighbour b.
planets.question: Is it another Venus?
planets.answer: It receives strong starlight, but its thermal observations disfavor a thick greenhouse atmosphere. A bare surface or a thinner, weak-greenhouse atmosphere remains possible.
planets.interior: Rocky crust and mantle with an iron-bearing core as a schematic possibility. No observed Venus-like atmosphere.
planets.evidence: The thermal phase curve measures dayside brightness and constrains nightside emission. Atmospheric models test whether a thick envelope fits.
planets.limits: Do not label oxygen as detected. The possible O2-rich atmosphere is one model interpretation.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 e
planets.hook: A small planet in a temperate orbit
planets.intro: TRAPPIST-1 e is slightly smaller than Earth, with a year lasting about six days. It receives enough starlight for liquid water to be possible with a suitable atmosphere. Whether it has air or water remains open, so both bare rock and a milder world are still possibilities.
planets.question: Why is the star part of the problem?
planets.answer: Bright and dark regions on the star change the light we measure during a transit. That can imitate or obscure features from the planet’s atmosphere, so repeated observations are needed.
planets.interior: Rock-and-iron interior constrained by mass and radius. Any water layer or substantial atmosphere must be a separately selected possible model.
planets.evidence: Four JWST transmission observations show changing stellar contamination. Atmospheric analyses allow both bare rock and some heavier-gas atmospheres.
planets.limits: There is no strong evidence for or against a secondary atmosphere in the cited analysis. Habitable-zone placement does not establish habitability.

planets.name: LHS 1140 b
planets.hook: A possible water-rich world
planets.intro: LHS 1140 b circles a cool star in about 25 days. Larger and heavier than Earth, it could hold a deep layer of water. One possible landscape is a frozen ocean with an open patch on the warmer day side. Far below, pressure could turn the water into dense ice above the rocky interior.
planets.question: Could an ocean have ice underneath it?
planets.answer: At great depth, pressure can turn water into dense forms of ice even when it is warm. A sufficiently water-rich planet could have these layers between an ocean and its rocky interior.
planets.interior: For the water-rich scenario: possible atmosphere → water or ice → high-pressure water phases → rock and iron. Retain an alternative envelope model in the research notes.
planets.evidence: Mass, radius and transmission spectra constrain the possible interior and atmosphere. Climate models provide the basis for an ice-and-ocean scene.
planets.limits: An ocean is not detected. Recent helium-escape claims face multiple JWST non-detections. Do not mark helium, nitrogen or a specific surface state as confirmed. The type-filter assignment needs an agreed rule for water-rich candidates.

planets.name: K2-18 b
planets.hook: Methane above an unresolved interior
planets.intro: K2-18 b has a hydrogen-rich atmosphere containing methane. Beneath it, a deep ocean is one possibility. Another is a much hotter interior under a thick envelope of gas. We do not yet know whether this planet has a liquid surface at all.
planets.question: What happened to the claims about life?
planets.answer: Some analyses reported possible sulfur-bearing molecules. Independent reanalyses found that the evidence was not robust and that other molecules could explain the features. Methane is a firmer part of the atmospheric picture.
planets.interior: Hydrogen-rich atmosphere → deep volatile envelope → uncertain water-rich or hotter deep region → rock/iron interior. Explain alternative structures rather than draw one confirmed ocean floor.
planets.evidence: Transmission spectra probe gases high in the atmosphere. Comparing reductions and molecular models tests which claimed features are robust.
planets.limits: No confirmed biosignature, ocean or inhabited surface. Include the original claim and independent challenges together. Avoid saying all carbon-bearing species are equally secure.

planets.name: HR 8799 e
planets.hook: A young giant we can separate from its star
planets.intro: HR 8799 e is a young gas giant still glowing with heat left over from its formation. It belongs to a family of four giant planets on wide orbits around the same star. Beneath its clouds lies a hot, dense interior that will cool over millions of years.
planets.question: What can four planets tell us that one cannot?
planets.answer: They share a star and formation environment. Differences in their atmospheric chemistry can help test how much gas and solid material each planet collected.
planets.interior: Cloudy atmosphere → hot hydrogen–helium fluid envelope → uncertain heavy-element distribution. Formation and atmospheric chemistry do not uniquely determine a solid core.
planets.evidence: Direct imaging separates the planets from stellar light. Spectroscopy measures molecular absorption, while orbital motion and stellar acceleration constrain mass.
planets.limits: Do not put its intrinsic effective temperature on the same unqualified cold-to-hot scale as equilibrium temperatures. Modelled radius is not a transit measurement. Slow orbital motion at 1 day per second is expected.

planets.name: 51 Eridani b
planets.hook: Methane in a young giant’s own light
planets.intro: 51 Eridani b is a young gas giant with methane and water vapour in its cloudy atmosphere. It still gives off heat from its formation, even far from its star. Deep below the clouds, increasing pressure turns the gas into dense fluid.
planets.question: Why do methane and carbon monoxide matter together?
planets.answer: Their relative amounts depend on temperature and how rapidly gas moves between layers. Seeing both helps test whether mixing carries gas upward faster than chemical reactions can adjust.
planets.interior: Cloudy atmosphere → warm, internally heated fluid envelope → uncertain deep composition. Layer sizes and radius are model-dependent.

planets.name: Beta Pictoris b
planets.hook: A giant with a roughly nine-hour spin
planets.intro: Beta Pictoris b is a young, hot giant that may spin once in roughly nine hours. It circles a star surrounded by a broad disc of dust, with another giant planet closer in. Heat left over from its formation keeps its atmosphere hot despite the distant star.
planets.question: How do you measure a planet’s spin?
planets.answer: One side of a rotating planet moves toward us while the other moves away. This broadens molecular lines in its spectrum. Converting the broadening into a period also requires a radius and an assumed viewing angle.
planets.interior: Young hot atmosphere → dense fluid envelope → uncertain heavy-element interior. No rocky exterior or measured core boundary.
planets.evidence: High-resolution molecular spectroscopy measures rotational broadening. Imaging, radial velocities and astrometry constrain the system.
planets.limits: The 8.7 ± 0.8 hour estimate assumes no obliquity in the cited analysis. It is not an exact observed solar day. Keep effective temperature separate from stellar-heating temperature.

planets.name: 51 Peg b
planets.hook: Hot gas above a hidden interior
planets.intro: 51 Peg b is a hot giant with water vapour in its atmosphere. It circles a Sun-like star in just over four days. Because it does not transit the star, its physical size is harder to measure.
planets.interior: A hydrogen–helium envelope grows denser with depth, passing into compressed fluid. Heavier elements may be concentrated near the centre or mixed through the deep interior.
planets.evidence: Motion of the planet or its host star constrains the orbit and mass. A radial-velocity mass may be a lower bound because the tilt of the orbit is not known. Direct-imaging radii depend on atmospheric or evolutionary models. The linked studies support the additional description and question below.

planets.name: Proxima Centauri b
planets.hook: A compact rocky world
planets.intro: A year on Proxima Centauri b lasts 11.2 days. It contains at least roughly 1.1 Earth masses. Rock and metal are plausible ingredients of its interior.
planets.question: Who are its neighbours?
planets.answer: Proxima Cen has 2 confirmed planets in this archive snapshot. Their orbital periods and distances are listed in the system view. A shared star can host planets of very different sizes.
planets.interior: A possible rocky interior contains an outer layer of rock, a deeper mantle and a metal-rich core. The measured size and mass constrain their proportions, but do not give a unique set of layer thicknesses.
planets.evidence: Motion of the planet or its host star constrains the orbit and mass. A radial-velocity mass may be a lower bound because the tilt of the orbit is not known. Direct-imaging radii depend on atmospheric or evolutionary models.
